source.title: On the Limits of Scale: Inverse Scaling in Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Rohit Saxena; Alessandro Suglia; Marek Rei; Pasquale Minervini

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some extracted tables have flattened or disrupted layout, but the reported results used here remain readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether downstream task accuracy improves consistently with model size, using benchmark accuracy and paired question outcomes rather than held-out pretraining loss or power-law fitting.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own VLM benchmark accuracy and inverse-scaling results. It also cites external scaling results and Qwen3-VL technical-report scores; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Accuracy values used only to define a case-selection threshold are not separate rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures downstream benchmark accuracy across released model sizes in four VLM families. It reports where accuracy does not improve with size, so its results bear on whether V6 holds at subtask level. It is not an original source. No loss or power-law fits are reported, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find aggregate VLM accuracy largely improves with size, but 375 subtask-level cases (3.6% of comparisons) show smaller models beating larger same-family ones. These replicate across families (13 subtasks in ≥3 families), persist in dense-only pairs, and are attenuated but not removed by CoT. They call the pattern task-driven, note it is observational and recipe-confounded, and recommend task-aware model selection.
record.recipe_differences: Uses benchmark accuracy and paired per-question flips on released VLM checkpoints, rather than fitting held-out language-model cross-entropy power laws or deriving compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Results depend on benchmark/subtask and prompting condition. CoT reduced the median Net from +8 to 0 and changed persistence rates substantially by benchmark. Option reordering modulated the six strongest BLINK cases but did not reverse their net advantage in the reported reruns.

fits_no_version.finding: The inverse-scaling case count depends on how model size is counted. With total parameters ≥2× there are 326 cases; with active parameters ≥2× there are 239, and BLINK falls from 95 to 58 cases. MoE models frequently appear as the 'larger' model in failing pairs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream-accuracy scaling trends in MoE/dense model families depend on whether size is counted as total or active parameters.

record.problems: Observational comparisons among released checkpoints cannot isolate parameter count from differences in language backbone, vision encoder, training data, alignment, active parameters, and other recipe details. Only open-weight models are included. Cases are selected using the same observed data with Net ≥ 5 and n ≥ 20; significance tests are exploratory and involve many overlapping comparisons. Accuracy gaps are benchmark- and subtask-specific, and some may be affected by benchmark annotation issues, option order, or size-dependent contamination.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix C lists all 375 individual cases; only the overall and benchmark aggregates plus the ten strongest cases in Table 3 were extracted here. Other individual case rows, detailed family-by-benchmark cells, the full robustness-threshold tables, and option-order rerun values were left out to keep the record compact; the paper reports these in Appendices C, F, I, and J. The key dense-only aggregate and CoT conditions are included.

untested.parts: No prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss. No fitted scaling curve or forecast of larger models. Model sizes differ in data, encoder and recipe, so scale is not isolated.
VLMs are evaluated, but no power-law form is fitted for any modality or regime.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits are compared across fitting choices.

missing.what: Aggregate benchmark accuracy per model: mostly monotonic, with exceptions. Qwen 30B-A3B scores 62.4% vs 4B 66.4% on BLINK; Molmo 4B beats 8B on BLINK (63.5 vs 59.3) and MMBench.
Smallest vs largest model per family: smaller ahead by Net ≥ 5 in only 9 of 666 comparisons.
Restrictions to ≥2× total parameters (326/9768, 3.3%) and ≥2× active parameters (239/8214, 2.9%). Under the active-parameter restriction the larger model is ahead by Net ≤ −5 in 51.0% of comparisons.
Larger model ahead by Net ≤ −5 in 47.9% of comparisons, with 2,478 significant under BH.
Same-encoder-tier restriction: 271 of 375 cases remain, and 10 of 13 replicated subtasks.
Option-order reruns of the six BLINK top cases: Net stays positive in all 17 runs; identity replays vary by up to 11 Net.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T5: the study's results argue V6 needs qualifying at subtask granularity, rather than retesting it as stated. Case selection uses the same data as the tests, and the top-10 rows are extremes. Released checkpoints differ in encoder, data and alignment, so these are not clean scale manipulations. Row counts of exceptions were relabelled from 'observed' to 'partial' relative to V6.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss or loss-versus-parameters, tokens, or compute power-law measurements.
No small-run loss-law fits or predictions of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute-budget comparison or estimate of compute-optimal parameter and token allocations.
No controlled comparisons isolating depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The evaluated systems are vision-language models, but the study does not test whether a power-law loss form transfers to other modalities or training regimes.
Tests benchmark accuracy across model sizes in VLM families, not downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss, nor whether a fitted predictor forecasts downstream performance.

No fitted loss-law exponents or compute-optimal split are compared across fitting choices. The study reports non-monotonic task-accuracy curves, not departures from fitted pretraining-loss power laws.

rows.measure: Eligible within-family model-pair/subtask cases with smaller-model advantage
rows.value: 375 cases out of 10,434 eligible comparisons; 115 subtask–dataset pairs

rows.note: A case is a (subtask, smaller model, larger model) tuple meeting the stated net-flip and sample-size thresholds.
rows.check: 'Observed' is ambiguous for V6. The row counts exceptions to scaling: 375 of 10,434 comparisons (3.6%) favour the smaller model. Scaling holds in most comparisons and fails in a minority, so relative to V6 this is partial.

relationships.condition: Aggregate benchmark accuracy and most within-family comparisons; widest size gaps
relationships.reason: Larger model ahead in 74.8% of comparisons (r02). From the text (not in rows): smallest-vs-largest model has the smaller ahead in only 9/666 comparisons, and the largest model is best or near-best on most benchmarks (Appendix B).
relationships.display_finding: Larger models led in 74.8% of comparisons, while the smallest model beat the largest in only 9 of 666 comparisons.

relationships.condition: Subtask level, all four families, direct prompting
relationships.reason: 3.6% of comparisons show smaller-model advantage at Net ≥ 5, concentrated in BLINK/MMT-Bench/MME, and many subtask curves are non-monotonic (r01, r03–r11, r22–r26). The count also depends on total vs active parameter ordering (text, Appendix I).
relationships.display_finding: Smaller models had a net advantage of at least five in 3.6% of comparisons, concentrated in BLINK, MMT-Bench and MME, with many non-monotonic curves and results sensitive to total versus active parameter ordering.

relationships.reason: The reversals depend on prompting. Under CoT, median Net falls from +8 to 0 and 101 of 375 cases flip to favour the larger model. Still, 25.6% persist, varying 7.1–48.6% by benchmark (r27–r36).
relationships.display_finding: Chain-of-thought prompting reduced the median net advantage for smaller models from +8 to zero and flipped 101 of 375 cases toward larger models, although 25.6% of reversals persisted, ranging from 7.1% to 48.6% across benchmarks.

relationships.condition: Specific subtasks and pairs (BLINK Jigsaw, Multi-view Reasoning, Forensic Detection; MME Landmark; ScienceQA Economics), direct prompting
relationships.reason: Smaller models beat larger same-family models by 7–39pp. In the Forensic Detection cases FlipNorm = 0 (r12–r21). These are released checkpoints with recipe confounds.
relationships.display_finding: Smaller same-family models led by 7–39 percentage points, with FlipNorm=0 in Forensic Detection cases, although checkpoint training differences confound size.
